questions.q: Per the real answer given in class, where does the actual logic for buying/selling a token live?
options: Built into the token contract itself — exchanges are just intermediaries using its public functions
Inside a separate government-run ledger
Nowhere — buying tokens is impossible on Ethereum
Only inside Ethereum's core protocol code, unrelated to any contract
questions.explain: The instructor was direct: the built code that facilitates buying is built into the contract itself, and exchanges just use its existing public methods.

questions.q: What does the token contract built in this chapter honestly NOT support, per this lesson?
options: Buying or selling the token for ETH directly through the contract — there's no built-in marketplace or pricing logic
Minting tokens
Transferring tokens between addresses
Approving an allowance for another address
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit about this real limitation: the contract only supports minting, transferring, and approving allowances — no built-in buy/sell logic.

questions.q: What real, additional step actually makes a deployed ERC-20 token tradeable on a DEX like Uniswap?
options: Adding a liquidity pool for the token on the DEX after deployment
Nothing — deployment alone makes it instantly tradeable everywhere
Renaming the token's symbol
Increasing the token's decimals value
questions.explain: Per the lesson, after deploying the ERC-20 token, you add a liquidity pool on a DEX like Uniswap — only then can users actually buy or sell it through that platform's interface.

questions.q: What does `constructor(uint initialSupply) { _mint(msg.sender, initialSupply); }` actually do?
options: Mints the entire starting token supply directly to whoever deploys the contract
Mints tokens to a random address
Prevents any tokens from ever being minted
Automatically lists the token on an exchange
questions.explain: This real, common pattern gives the token a starting supply in the very same transaction that deploys the contract, minted straight to the deployer.

questions.q: How does a centralized exchange like Coinbase actually let people buy and sell a listed token, per this lesson?
options: It builds its own buy/sell system on top of the token contract's existing public functions
It rewrites the token's smart contract entirely
It has no real connection to the token's actual contract
It only works with tokens that have no public functions at all
questions.explain: Centralized exchanges act as intermediaries: their buy/sell mechanisms are hooked up to the token's real contract and its existing public methods, same as any other user of the contract.
